stimulus.title: Mini-model (teacher reads aloud)
paragraphs: A: I'll do the introduction, and you can do the results. B: Fine. Shall I make the slides too? A: Yes, please. Oh, and actually, could you take the introduction as well? You know the background better than I do. B: Sure.

items.prompt: Who will give the introduction? Speaker A / Speaker B
items.evidence: could you take the introduction as well?
items.reason: The answer is delayed: A first offers to do it, then changes the plan several lines later.

blocks.title: Predict before you listen
blocks.instructions: Look at the notes for Recording 1. What type of word is needed in each gap? Write A for a noun, B for an adjective or adverb in comparative form, or C for a verb.

items.prompt: Separate lines: customers frustrated when another line moved ________
items.evidence: 'moved ...' needs a word describing how: a comparative such as quicker or slower.
items.reason: After 'moved', a comparison with their own line is expected.

items.prompt: Offices put ________ beside lift doors
items.evidence: 'put ... beside' needs a thing: a noun, probably plural.
items.reason: Check plural: 'put ... beside lift doors' suggests more than one.

items.prompt: Queue-jumping produces ________ out of proportion to the time lost
items.evidence: 'produces ...' needs a noun: what is produced.
items.reason: A feeling or reaction is likely; listen for a noun.

blocks.title: The design of queues
blocks.mode: Guided listening practice: one play under practice conditions, then teacher-controlled review
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-10: complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.
blocks.form_title: The design of queues: lecture notes

stimulus.title: Recording IELTS-10-L1 transcript (teacher-private)
paragraphs: LECTURER: Good morning, everyone. In today's lecture I want to look at something we all experience but rarely think about: waiting in queues. Businesses spend a surprising amount of effort designing how we wait, and the research behind these designs tells us a lot about how people perceive time.

LECTURER: Let's start with the shape of the queue itself. Many banks and post offices once had a separate line for each counter. The problem was that customers kept comparing their own line with the others, and they became frustrated whenever another line moved faster. A single line feeding several counters solves this. The average wait may be almost the same, but people consider the system fairer, and that sense of fairness makes the wait easier to accept.

LECTURER: This leads to an important point. What matters to customers is often not the actual length of the wait, but how long it feels. Last term I tried an informal poll with one of my seminar groups. I asked them to guess how long they had queued in the canteen that day, and then we compared their guesses with the times on their receipts. I'd predicted that the guesses would be about fifty per cent too long, but in fact most people guessed roughly double their real wait. That was one small group, so treat it as an illustration rather than a research finding, but it does show how unreliable our sense of waiting time can be. So the question for designers is what makes a wait feel longer than it really is, and several factors stand out.

LECTURER: The first is having nothing to do. Unoccupied time drags. A well-known example comes from office buildings where people complained that the lifts were too slow. Rather than install faster lifts, which would have been expensive, managers put mirrors beside the lift doors. People spent the time checking their appearance, and the complaints largely stopped, even though the lifts were no faster.

LECTURER: The second factor is uncertainty. If you don't know how long you'll be waiting, every minute seems longer. That's why many theme parks and call centres now display or announce an estimated waiting time. Interestingly, some organisations deliberately make that estimate a little longer than they expect the wait to be, so that customers are pleasantly surprised when they're served early.

LECTURER: Third, unexplained waits feel longer than explained ones. Passengers on a delayed train are far more patient when the driver gives the reason for the delay, even if the news itself is bad. Silence, on the other hand, tends to make people imagine the worst.

LECTURER: The fourth factor concerns the stage of the process. Waiting before a service begins feels longer than waiting once it has started. Restaurants understand this very well. Rather than leaving customers standing by the door until a table is ready, they often hand them a menu, because once you're choosing your meal, you feel the experience has already begun.

LECTURER: A further factor, and one that is easy to overlook, is company. People who wait alone consistently report the time as longer than people who wait with friends or family. Conversation, it seems, is a natural distraction, and it works even between strangers: in some studies, simply seating people so that they faced one another made the wait feel shorter.

LECTURER: The last factor, and perhaps the most powerful, is fairness. People will tolerate a long wait if everyone is treated equally, but even a short wait becomes unbearable if someone pushes in. Seeing someone jump the queue produces anger out of all proportion to the time actually lost.

LECTURER: Finally, let's think about the future of queuing. Increasingly, the line itself is disappearing. In virtual queues, customers register when they arrive and are then told when it's their turn. Early systems handed out electronic pagers, but so many of these went missing that most venues now simply send a message to the customer's own phone. This allows people to shop, eat or simply sit down instead of standing in line. It doesn't remove the wait, of course, but it changes how the wait feels, which, as we've seen, is what really matters.
LECTURER: In the next lecture, we'll look at how these ideas have been applied in hospitals, where waiting can be a matter of health rather than convenience.

items.prompt: Separate lines: customers frustrated when another line moved ________
items.evidence: they became frustrated whenever another line moved faster
items.reason: The comparison with their own line is the source of frustration.

items.prompt: Single line: average wait similar, but system seen as ________
items.evidence: people consider the system fairer
items.reason: 'Seen as' paraphrases 'consider'.

items.prompt: Lecturer's class poll: most guesses were about ________ the real waiting time
items.evidence: most people guessed roughly double their real wait
items.reason: 'Fifty per cent' comes first but is only what the lecturer predicted; 'in fact' introduces the result. The lecturer frames the poll as an illustration, not research.

items.prompt: Nothing to do: offices put ________ beside lift doors
items.evidence: managers put mirrors beside the lift doors
items.reason: Faster lifts were considered but rejected as too expensive.

items.prompt: Uncertainty: some organisations make their estimates intentionally ________ than the expected wait
items.evidence: deliberately make that estimate a little longer than they expect the wait to be
items.reason: 'Intentionally' paraphrases 'deliberately'. The answer is the relationship between the estimate and the real wait, not the word 'time'.

items.prompt: Unexplained waits: with no information, passengers tend to imagine the ________
items.evidence: Silence, on the other hand, tends to make people imagine the worst
items.reason: 'With no information' paraphrases 'silence'. 'Reason' is heard first but describes the opposite case (an explained delay).

items.prompt: Before service begins: restaurants give waiting customers a ________
items.evidence: they often hand them a menu
items.reason: A table is mentioned, but customers are waiting for it; the menu is what they are given.

items.prompt: Company: waiting ________ feels longer than waiting with others
items.evidence: People who wait alone consistently report the time as longer
items.reason: 'Feels longer' paraphrases 'report the time as longer'.

items.prompt: Fairness: queue-jumping produces ________ out of proportion to time lost
items.evidence: produces anger out of all proportion to the time actually lost
items.reason: The note paraphrases the lecturer's sentence closely; spelling must be correct.

items.prompt: Future: early virtual queues used pagers, but many were ________
items.evidence: so many of these went missing
items.reason: The problem with pagers explains why phones replaced them. 'Phone' is heard next but is the solution, not the problem.

stages.title: Opening challenge: the delayed answer
stages.student: Listen to a short exchange read aloud once and answer the question.
stages.teacher: Read the mini-model once at natural speed. Ask when the answer changed. Connect to Lesson 5: in longer recordings, corrections can come several sentences later.
stages.say: In Parts 3 and 4, the answer may come later than you expect. Keep listening.
stages.check: Learners can say which words changed the plan.

stages.title: Signposts and prediction
stages.student: Predict the word type for three gaps, then check. Copy the signpost list: first, the second factor, third, the fourth factor, fifth, finally.
stages.teacher: Teach how Part 4 lectures are organised by signposts, and how notes follow the same order. Reveal prediction answers after learners commit.
stages.say: Signposts tell you which part of the notes you are in. If you miss one answer, the next signpost helps you catch up.

stages.title: Prepare for the lecture
stages.student: Read Questions 1-10. Predict the word type for every gap.
stages.teacher: The recording gives 30 seconds of reading time; allow up to 2 more minutes for prediction. Foundation learners use the printed word-type hints.
stages.say: ONE WORD ONLY. Two words will be marked wrong, even if the meaning is correct.
stages.check: Each learner has a prediction beside most gaps.

stages.title: The lecture: one play
stages.student: Listen once and complete the notes.
stages.teacher: Play IELTS-10-L1 once without pausing. If audio fails, stop and use Plan B; never read the transcript as a substitute.
stages.say: Follow the signposts. If you miss a gap, move on.
stages.check: All answers committed before the review.

stages.title: Review: answers, distractors and spelling
stages.student: Check answers. Mark spelling and word-limit errors separately from listening errors. Keep your first answers visible.
stages.teacher: Reveal in pairs. Ask what the lecturer said before the answer for Q3 (fifty per cent was only the prediction), Q4 (faster lifts), Q6 (reason) and Q10 (phone). Optional teacher-controlled second play with pauses at signposts for foundation learners, recorded as support.
stages.say: Mentioned is not the same as the answer. Faster lifts were mentioned and rejected.
stages.check: Learners can explain the distractor for Q3 or Q4.

stages.title: From notes to summary
stages.student: Using only your notes, write a three-sentence summary of the lecture: the main idea, two examples, and the conclusion about virtual queues.
stages.teacher: Model the first sentence aloud: 'The lecture argues that how long a wait feels matters more than how long it is.' High-band learners write without the model sentence.
stages.say: Good notes let you rebuild the whole argument.
stages.check: Each learner has a summary of three sentences.

stages.title: Peer check and second listen
stages.student: Compare summaries with a partner. Listen to the lecture once more (guided review) and add anything important you missed.
stages.teacher: Play the recording again as guided review only. This second play is practice and is recorded as such.
stages.say: Listen for anything that would change your summary.
stages.check: Pairs have added at least one point.

stages.title: My listening log
stages.student: In the log at the end of the workbook, record each wrong answer as a listening, spelling or word-limit error, and set one target.
stages.teacher: Note the error types learners actually record. No band conversion.
stages.say: Spelling and word limits are easy marks to protect.

stages.title: Exit ticket and homework
stages.student: Complete the exit ticket and take the homework sheet.
stages.teacher: Collect exit tickets. Assign online practice only through the existing workflow. Record the fresh-check date.
stages.say: Next lesson: describing charts in Writing Task 1.
stages.check: Everyone knows the homework and check date.

blocks.title: How migrating birds find their way
blocks.instructions: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

stimulus.title: Recording IELTS-10-C1 transcript (teacher-private)
paragraphs: LECTURER: This afternoon I'd like to consider a question that has puzzled people for centuries: how do migrating birds find their way across thousands of kilometres? The short answer is that they don't rely on a single method. Instead, they combine several cues.
LECTURER: During the day, many species use the position of the sun. Because the sun moves across the sky, birds must adjust for the time of day, and they appear to do this using an internal clock.

LECTURER: Many songbirds migrate at night, however, and for them the stars are important. Some of the clearest evidence came from experiments in planetariums, where researchers could change the pattern of stars on the ceiling and watch the birds change the direction they tried to fly.
LECTURER: Birds can also sense the Earth's magnetic field. This is particularly useful because, unlike the sun or the stars, it can still be detected under heavy cloud.

LECTURER: As they approach their destination, birds increasingly rely on landmarks such as coastlines, rivers and mountain ranges. And some seabirds seem to use smell to locate the small islands where they nest.

LECTURER: One final point. Young birds on their first migration usually set off in roughly the right direction, but if strong winds push them off course, they often fail to correct it. Experienced adults, by contrast, can usually find their way back, which suggests that navigation is partly learned rather than entirely inherited.

items.prompt: By day: birds use the position of the ________
items.evidence: many species use the position of the sun
items.reason: Direct detail after the 'during the day' signpost.

items.prompt: At night: star use shown in experiments in ________
items.evidence: experiments in planetariums
items.reason: Spelling must be correct.

items.prompt: Magnetic field: works even under heavy ________
items.evidence: it can still be detected under heavy cloud
items.reason: Contrasted with the sun and stars, which clouds hide.

items.prompt: Near the destination: birds use ________ such as coastlines and rivers
items.evidence: rely on landmarks such as coastlines, rivers and mountain ranges
items.reason: The examples follow the answer word.

items.prompt: Some seabirds use ________ to locate their nesting islands
items.evidence: some seabirds seem to use smell to locate the small islands
items.reason: Direct detail; 'nesting islands' paraphrases 'islands where they nest'.

items.prompt: Young birds often fail to correct being pushed off ________ by wind
items.evidence: if strong winds push them off course, they often fail to correct it
items.reason: 'Off course' is the fixed phrase; 'direction' appears earlier but does not fit the gap.
